summary.one_line: A southern-India, backward-integrated secondary steel maker (sponge iron to TMT bars, coils and pipes) with a volatile, thin-margin earnings record, raising Rs 355 cr of fresh money mostly to repay debt, and carrying several governance flags from promoter-group dealings around its NCLT-acquired subsidiary Basai Steels.
bull_points: Real backward integration: in FY26 it used 82.35% of its own sponge iron and 98.89% of its own MS billets in-house, across six plants with 17,33,100 MTPA installed capacity (S24, S5).
FY26 was a strong year: revenue from operations of Rs 4,148.57 cr (up from Rs 3,541.78 cr) and PAT of Rs 127.41 cr against Rs 7.71 cr in FY25; EBITDA was Rs 303.64 cr (S5, S4).
Low customer concentration: the largest customer was 5.33% and the top 10 were 27.90% of FY26 revenue from operations (S6, S8).
Cheap green power: 83.20% of electricity came from renewable sources in FY26, from about 230 MW of solar and wind PPAs, with a stated saving of Rs 1.57 per unit (S5, S15).
Rs 250 cr of the fresh issue repays debt, which is 28.92% of the Rs 864.41 cr standalone borrowings as of July 15, 2026 (S20).
bear_points: Earnings have been volatile. PAT went Rs 38.91 cr, then Rs 7.71 cr, then Rs 127.41 cr over FY24-FY26. Operating cash flow fell the other way, from Rs 325.40 cr to Rs 108.96 cr to Rs 62.80 cr (S6).
About half of FY26 sales (49.99%) were trading and intermediary sales, i.e. semi-finished products plus traded coal, iron ore and steel. Only 50.01% came through finished-product channels (S13).

Governance flags around the subsidiary Basai Steels. There are NCLT oppression and liquidation petitions by its erstwhile promoter. 13.03 acres of Basai land were sold for Rs 26.06 lakh to promoter-group entity A-One Defence and Aerospace, and Moneylife reports the RHP does not separately disclose that sale (S3, S7).
The company gave a Rs 185 cr corporate guarantee to SBI for A-One Defence and Aerospace, a promoter-group entity incorporated in May 2025 (S7, S26).

The company, its promoters and its officers paid Companies Act penalties of roughly Rs 46 lakh between 2019 and 2025 for lapses in accounts, board reports, KMP appointments and vigil-mechanism disclosure (S25).
watch_points: The Bellary Facility I lease from Basai: Moneylife reports the registered deed runs only to June 30, 2026, while the RHP describes a 9+3 year term and the DRHP had said 30 years (S7).
Outcome of the NCLT Hyderabad petitions (CP 29/241/HDB/2025 and the liquidation IA 975/2025) and of the Basai-A-One amalgamation scheme (S3, S7).
Whether operating cash flow recovers towards reported profit in FY27. Trade receivables were Rs 664.46 cr at March 31, 2026 (S22, S6).
Final subscription mix on September 28. No category-wise figures were available on day 1 (S23).

reasoning: The fresh money does not fund growth. The DRHP earmarked Rs 344.37 cr for Koppal/Vanya expansion capex and Rs 40 cr for captive solar (S9, S11). The RHP cut the fresh issue to Rs 355 cr, with Rs 250 cr going to debt prepayment and the rest to general corporate purposes (S20, S21). Rs 50 cr of the total is an OFS that goes to the promoters (S4). Any expansion is therefore left to be funded with debt or internal accruals (S14).

There is no durable moat. This is a regional secondary-steel producer: 54.86% of revenue comes from Karnataka, raw materials take 84.05% of revenue, and half of sales are intermediate or traded goods (S13, S24). Integration and cheap green power are genuine cost advantages, but they are not barriers a competitor cannot replicate.

Earnings quality is weak. FY26 PAT of Rs 127.41 cr came after two years averaging about Rs 23 cr, and FY26 operating cash flow was only Rs 62.80 cr (S6). The growth story rests on a single year that the cash flow does not yet confirm.

Governance is the deciding negative. Basai Steels was acquired through an NCLT resolution plan and is now the subject of oppression and liquidation petitions (S3). One petition alleges the approved equity infusion of Rs 127.73 cr has not materialised (S3). Basai land went to a promoter-group company for Rs 26.06 lakh for 13.03 acres (S7). The listed-to-be company guarantees Rs 185 cr of a new promoter entity's bank debt (S7). The company has a record of repeated Companies Act penalties (S25).
For a retail investor, the sensible course is to stay out and revisit only after a few listed quarters that show cash conversion and a clean resolution of the Basai matters (S7, S6).

subsections.title: What the company makes and how the chain fits together

blocks.text: A-One Steels India was incorporated in April 2012 as A-One Steel and Alloys Private Limited. It began commercial production in 2013 with MS billets at Gauribidanur, and was converted to a public company in December 2024 (S8, S27, S3). It describes itself as a backward-integrated steel maker. Iron ore is converted into sponge iron in coal-based kilns. Sponge iron is melted into MS billets. Billets are rolled into long products (TMT bars) and flat products (HR and CR coils), and coils are further converted into HR and CR pipes and galvanised tubes. It also makes met coke and ferro alloys (silicon manganese, ferrosilicon) as industrial products (S5, S15, S27).

The integration is real rather than cosmetic. In FY26 the company consumed 82.35% of its own sponge iron, 98.89% of its MS billets and 88.81% of its coils in-house (S24). That matters because the margin in secondary steel sits in the conversion spread between raw material and finished product. Owning each step captures more of that spread, but it also means the company absorbs every swing in iron ore and coal prices. Raw material costs consumed 84.05% of revenue (S24).

items: Brand: finished long products are sold under the 'A-One Gold' brand (S6, S10).
Certifications cited: 5-star green steel rating from the Ministry of Steel, and CII green-product certification for TMT bars (S27).
Workforce: 1,377 permanent employees and 1,082 contract workers (S22, S8).

blocks.text: In plain terms, this is a secondary (coal-based DRI / induction-furnace route) steel producer that sells both finished steel and a large volume of semi-finished and traded material. It is not a specialty-steel or import-substitution story.

The company operates six manufacturing units. Five are in Karnataka: Gauribidanur, two at Bellary, Koppal and Chikkantapur. One is at Hindupur in Andhra Pradesh. Together they cover about 401.75 acres (S24, S27). Aggregate installed capacity for intermediate, finished and industrial products was 17,33,100 MTPA at March 31, 2026 (S5, S15). That is up from 14.97 lakh MTPA at June 2024 as stated in the DRHP (S9). The plants are sited near the Bellary-Koppal iron ore belt and within about 450 km of the Ennore, New Mangalore and Mormugao ports, which matter for imported coal (S8, S27).

blocks.caption: FY26 capacity utilisation by product and plant (as reported in secondary summaries of the RHP)

blocks.text: Upstream capacity (sponge iron, billets, coke) is effectively full, and the only real slack is in TMT rolling at Hindupur. More volume from here needs new upstream capacity, and new upstream capacity needs capital. That is why the removal of the capex object from the IPO (see issue details) matters.

Bellary Facility I is one of the plants running near full utilisation. It sits on land leased from subsidiary Basai Steels, and the term of that lease has been described differently across filings: 30 years in the DRHP, 9+3 years in the RHP, and a registered deed ending June 30, 2026 according to Moneylife's review (S7).

subsections.title: How revenue is earned: products, channels, geography, customers and suppliers

blocks.text: The channel split is the most revealing number in the business. 49.99% of FY26 sales were trading or intermediary sales, compared with 43.94% in FY25 and 51.89% in FY24 (S13). Intermediary sales are billets, coils and sponge iron sold to other mills. Trading sales are coal, iron ore, billets and steel bought and resold (S13). These are low-margin, price-taker revenues. The branded A-One Gold TMT business is a minority of sales, and its share fell in FY26 (S13).

Customer concentration is low. The largest customer was 5.33% and the top 10 customers were 27.90% of FY26 revenue from operations, across 1,715 customers in total (S6, S8, S13). Supplier concentration is higher: the top ten suppliers were about 49.24% of FY26 purchases (S29). Iron ore and coal are bought through domestic e-auctions, linkages and imports. Coking coal comes from Russia, South Africa, Australia and Canada, and steam coal from Indonesia and South Africa (S29).

Geography cuts both ways. Being close to Karnataka's ore belt and its construction market is a logistics advantage, but more than half of revenue depends on one state's construction cycle and one state's iron-ore mining policy (S13).

The RHP's industry section relies on a CRISIL report. It says domestic steel demand grew at an 11.6% CAGR between FY2021 and FY2026, moderating to 8% growth in FY2026. Finished steel demand is projected to grow at 6.5-8.5% a year between FY2027 and FY2031, to 227-237 million tonnes (S8). Infrastructure and construction account for nearly 65% of India's steel consumption (S8). That construction share is exactly the market for TMT bars and pipes.

Against that market, A-One's 17.33 lakh MTPA of aggregate capacity is small. The figure also mixes intermediate, finished and industrial products, so it is not a like-for-like crude-steel number (S5). The company is a regional player in a national commodity market whose prices are set by large integrated mills and by import parity.

Demand growth is a tailwind for the whole sector, not a specific advantage for A-One. Rising demand also attracts new capacity: large integrated producers such as those in Bellary are expanding in the same region.

The RHP's listed peer set is MSP Steel, Jai Balaji Industries and Shyam Metallics. All three are eastern-India secondary or integrated steel producers, and an independent review called the comparison weak because of limited comparability (S22). In its home market, A-One's real competition for TMT bars and pipes comes from national brands produced by large integrated mills and from dozens of regional secondary mills in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. For sponge iron and billets it sells into a commodity market with many producers.

items: Listed peers named in the RHP: MSP Steel, Jai Balaji Industries, Shyam Metallics (S22).
Revenue base for scale context: Rs 4,148.57 cr in FY26 (S5).
No market-share claim for any product was found in the RHP summaries reviewed.

blocks.text: Mostly no. The company has three genuine advantages. First, integration from sponge iron through to pipes, with high in-house consumption (S24). Second, proximity to the Bellary-Koppal ore belt and to ports (S8). Third, an unusually high renewable share of power, which CRISIL says is substantially higher than peers and which saves about Rs 1.57 per unit (S27, S5). Together these give a cost position that is probably better than many small regional mills.

None of these is a barrier. There is no import-substitution position, no 'only Indian maker' claim, no regulatory licence that keeps others out, and no pricing power. PAT margin was about 1% in FY24, 0.3% in FY25 and 3% in FY26 (S22). Half of revenue is intermediate or traded commodity (S13). Brand strength in A-One Gold TMT is regional, and the TMT share of revenue fell in FY26 (S13).

Verdict on the moat: this is a cost-position story in a cyclical commodity. It is not a franchise. The 'high industry barriers' language in the offer document (S6) describes capital intensity, which also caps returns.

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials, Rs crore (fiscal years ending March 31)
rows: EBITDA margin on revenue from ops (computed)

blocks.text: Revenue fell about 8% in FY25 and rose about 17% in FY26 (S19). In other words, the top line in FY26 was only about 8% above FY24 (computed from S6 and S5). The FY26 profit jump came mainly from margin, not volume. EBITDA rose 74% while revenue rose 17% (computed from S4, S5). ROE was 14.70% and ROCE 12.86% in FY26, compared with a RoCE of 8.67% in FY24 and 7.03% in FY25 (S10, S22). FY25 was hit by what the offer document attributes to geopolitical factors and ongoing expansion work (S22).

One good year, not a trend. Three years of history show PAT moving from Rs 38.91 cr to Rs 7.71 cr to Rs 127.41 cr (S4). Over that window, margins are what drove earnings, and margins in secondary steel follow the spread between steel prices and iron ore/coal prices, which the company does not control.

subsections.title: Cash flow and working capital: the profit-cash mismatch

blocks.text: Operating cash flow moved in the opposite direction to profit. It went from Rs 325.40 cr in FY24 to Rs 108.96 cr in FY25 to Rs 62.80 cr in FY26, while PAT went from Rs 38.91 cr to Rs 7.71 cr to Rs 127.41 cr (S6). Secondary reviews attribute the FY26 decline to rising inventory and trade receivables (S14). Trade receivables stood at Rs 664.46 cr at March 31, 2026 (S22). That is roughly 58 days of FY26 revenue from operations (computed from S22 and S5).

Across the three years combined, operating cash flow (about Rs 497 cr) still exceeds cumulative PAT (about Rs 174 cr), which is normal for a depreciation-heavy manufacturer (computed from S6). The problem is direction. In the year the company chose to go public, it converted only about half its reported profit into operating cash. That is the opposite of what a durable improvement looks like.
FY26 OCF of Rs 62.80 cr against PAT of Rs 127.41 cr (S6) is the single most important financial red flag. Before trusting the FY26 earnings step-up, look for FY27 cash conversion.

Total borrowings have stayed around Rs 1,000 cr for three years: Rs 1,042.53 cr, then Rs 963.67 cr, then Rs 1,010.94 cr (S4). Net worth nearly doubled over the same period, from Rs 421.79 cr to Rs 819.52 cr (S4). A pre-IPO equity raise and FY26 profit made debt-to-equity look healthier, at 1.17x in FY26 (S19, S10). Scanx reports a different measure improving from 4.39x to 2.70x (S6), so the ratio depends on the definition used. Standalone borrowings were Rs 864.41 cr at July 15, 2026: Rs 721.11 cr fund-based and Rs 143.30 cr non-fund-based (S20). About Rs 916.64 cr of borrowings are at variable rates (S6).

items: Contingent liabilities: Rs 108.97 cr (S22).
Corporate guarantee of Rs 185 cr given to SBI for promoter-group entity A-One Defence and Aerospace, disclosed as a subsequent event (S7).
Basai Steels has given a corporate guarantee to Bajaj Finance, and Bajaj Finance holds an exclusive charge over Basai's fixed assets (S7).
No dividends paid in the reported periods (S22).

blocks.text: Repaying Rs 250 cr would cut standalone debt by about 29% (S20) and lower interest cost. It de-risks the balance sheet, but it does not add capacity.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Offer structure at the upper band (Rs 405)
rows: Offer for sale - Krishan Kumar Jalan

items: Price band Rs 385-405, face value Rs 10, lot 37 shares, minimum retail application Rs 14,985 (S4).
Reservation: QIB not more than 50% (60% of it to anchors), retail not less than 35%, NII not less than 15%. There is an employee reservation of about Rs 2 cr at a Rs 38 discount (S4, S21, S18).
Dates: opens September 24, closes September 28, allotment September 29, listing October 1, 2026 on BSE and NSE (S4).
BRLMs: PL Capital Markets and Khambatta Securities. Registrar: Bigshare Services. Monitoring agency: a credit rating agency reporting quarterly (S4, S20).
Promoter holding falls from 85.86% to 74.52% (S4). Some summaries of the filing give the pre-issue figure as 85.56% (S26).

blocks.text: The Rs 50 cr OFS goes entirely to the three promoters. The company receives nothing from it (S4).

blocks.caption: Use of fresh-issue proceeds (RHP)
rows: Prepayment / partial repayment of certain borrowings (to be deployed in FY27)
General corporate purposes (capped at 25% of gross fresh issue)
Offer-related expenses (balance of the Rs 355 cr gross)

blocks.caption: Borrowings identified for repayment (outstanding as of July 15, 2026)

blocks.text: Much of the identified debt is working-capital lines at 8-9.6% (S20). Repaying working-capital lines with equity is effectively funding working capital permanently, and the lines can be redrawn. Several summaries (ipoji, a2zipo) still list Koppal/Vanya expansion capex and captive solar as objects (S11, S12). Those are the DRHP objects. The RHP-based reporting consistently shows only debt repayment and general corporate purposes (S5, S20, S21).

subsections.title: How the objects changed from DRHP to RHP

blocks.text: This change is central to the investment case. The IPO shrank by Rs 245 cr of fresh money, and the growth capex that justified the original filing was removed, while the debt-repayment slice rose 2.5x (S9, S20). Secondary reviews say the Koppal expansion is now to be debt-funded (S14). An investor applying today is therefore funding a balance-sheet repair and a promoter part-exit, not a new plant.
What the money raised is for: repaying debt and general corporate purposes, plus a Rs 50 cr promoter OFS. None of it is growth capital.

The promoters are Sandeep Kumar (Managing Director, 49, B.Com, 18+ years in steel), Sunil Jallan/Jalan (Chairman and Whole-time Director, 53, B.Com, 18+ years in steel) and Krishan Kumar Jalan (73, 16+ years in steel) (S27). Sunil Jalan and Sandeep Kumar are brothers (S26). Uma Shankar Goyanka is a Whole-time Director. The independent directors are Krishan Singh Barguzar, Kamaldeep Singh and Jeevika Poddar (S10). The company secretary is Pooja Sara Nagaraja (S3).

The promoters have built the business themselves over about 13 years, from one billet plant in 2013 to six units (S27). That is a genuine operating track record in the sector. The expansion has leaned heavily on acquiring distressed assets: Vanya Steels was acquired in 2017 (S29), and Basai Steels came through an NCLT resolution plan (S7). Promoters and promoter-group members have given personal guarantees reported at Rs 6,285.84 cr for borrowings of the company and its subsidiaries (S26, S8). That figure is far larger than the Rs 1,010.94 cr of reported consolidated borrowings (S4), and it could not be reconciled from the sources reviewed. The promoters have also extended unsecured loans of about Rs 13.77 cr to the company (S26).

subsections.title: Related-party dealings and the Basai Steels saga

blocks.text: The related-party picture is not routine, and most of it runs through Basai Steels and Power, a Hyderabad-registered company. A-One owns 78.14% of Basai (92.13 crore shares of Re 1) through an NCLT-approved resolution plan (S3, S7). Basai's other shareholders include Prem Enterprises (8.37%), Edelweiss ARC trusts (about 9.8% combined), the erstwhile promoter Gopal Agarwal (2.51%) and Canara Bank (1.02%), plus token holdings by promoter-family members (S3). Basai's Bellary land (131.91 acres) is leased to A-One and houses Bellary Facility I (S3, S7).

items: Oppression and mismanagement petition (CP 29/241/HDB/2025) by Gopal Agarwal against Basai and A-One, alleging misuse of powers and diversion of funds. It was pending as of September 15, 2026 (S3, S7).

Liquidation application (IA 975/2025). It alleges that the Rs 127.73 cr equity infusion required by the April 2018 resolution plan did not materialise, that A-One defaulted on lease rentals, and that A-One misrepresented itself as a strategic investor and wrongly called Basai a subsidiary in the DRHP (S3). A-One disputes this and says it has infused substantial funds (S3).
Canara Bank application seeking about Rs 1.99 cr plus 10.40% interest for delayed resolution-plan payment from Prem Enterprises and A-One (S3).

A dispute over 9.875 crore Basai shares between Prem Enterprises and K. Ravi Shankar, with an FIR alleging forged signatures (S3). K. Ravi Shankar also challenges the share-swap ratio in the proposed amalgamation (S7).
Basai tax proceedings of Rs 11,355.04 lakh (about Rs 113.55 cr): 7 direct-tax and 4 indirect-tax cases (S3).

On December 14, 2025, 13.03 acres of Basai land were sold to promoter-group entity A-One Defence and Aerospace (incorporated May 15, 2025) for Rs 26.06 lakh, i.e. about Rs 2 lakh an acre. An Edelweiss ARC valuation had put the land at Rs 8-12 lakh an acre. Moneylife reports the sale is not separately described in the RHP (S7).
A-One Steels gave a Rs 185 cr corporate guarantee to SBI for A-One Defence and Aerospace, and receives rental income and reimbursements from it (S7).
An amalgamation of Basai and A-One Gold Pipes & Tubes into A-One (board approval March 14, 2026; appointed date October 1, 2025) is before NCLT (S7).

blocks.text: A listed-to-be company guaranteeing Rs 185 cr of debt for a months-old promoter entity, while that same entity buys land from a partly-owned subsidiary at a fraction of an ARC valuation, is exactly the minority-shareholder risk that should decide the call (S7).

The offer document discloses Companies Act penalties paid by the company, its directors and officers between 2019 and 2025, totalling roughly Rs 46.15 lakh (S25). The company says all the disclosed matters are closed (S25).

blocks.caption: Companies Act penalties (as summarised from the RHP)

blocks.text: Individually these are small. Collectively they show a pattern of lapses in basic record-keeping and board process, covering books of account, financial statements, board reports and KMP appointment, and the most recent penalty was only in December 2025 (S25). Outstanding litigation involving the company was put at Rs 5,558.44 lakh (S6). Khambatta Securities, one of the BRLMs, handled 12 IPOs in three fiscal years, and 4 of them listed below the issue price (S22).

The governance record is below what a retail investor should accept in a thin-margin, leveraged commodity business, where minority shareholders depend on the promoters dealing fairly with group entities.

subsections.title: The risks that could change the decision

items: 1. Governance and related-party risk around Basai Steels and A-One Defence and Aerospace. This covers the NCLT oppression and liquidation petitions, the land sale to a promoter entity, and the Rs 185 cr guarantee (S3, S7).
2. Asset-security risk at Bellary Facility I. The plant is on land leased from Basai, the lease term is described inconsistently, and a liquidation petition against the lessor is pending (S7, S3).
3. Earnings volatility and commodity spread risk. PAT was Rs 38.91 cr, Rs 7.71 cr and Rs 127.41 cr over FY24-FY26, and raw materials take 84% of revenue (S4, S24).
4. Cash conversion and working capital. FY26 OCF was Rs 62.80 cr against PAT of Rs 127.41 cr, and receivables were Rs 664.46 cr (S6, S22).

5. Leverage and rate exposure. Borrowings are about Rs 1,011 cr, about Rs 916.64 cr is at variable rates, contingent liabilities are Rs 108.97 cr, and there are restrictive covenants (S4, S6, S22, S24).
6. Execution risk on growth now funded by debt. The capex objects were removed from the IPO while the Koppal expansion continues on borrowed money (S9, S14).
7. Geographic and regulatory concentration. 54.86% of revenue comes from Karnataka, and all plants depend on Karnataka/Andhra Pradesh ore and power policy (S13).
8. Revenue quality. About half of sales are low-margin intermediary and trading sales (S13).

blocks.text: Customer concentration is not a real risk here: the top customer was 5.33% of revenue (S6). Supplier concentration of about 49% with the top ten (S29) is typical for a commodity buyer of ore and coal. The risks that matter are the governance and cash-flow ones, not the boilerplate cyclicality language.
Risks 1, 2 and 4 are specific to this company and cannot be diversified away by owning the sector.

blocks.caption: Key disclosed proceedings
rows: Gopal Agarwal v. Basai, A-One and others (oppression)
Pending; alleges Rs 127.73 cr infusion unmet (S3)
About Rs 1.99 cr + 10.40% interest; under settlement (S3)
A-One defamation suit against Agarwal family and others

blocks.text: The Basai disputes involve overlapping corporate, civil, regulatory and criminal proceedings with common parties, including SEBI SCORES complaints and an FIR (S7). Resolution timelines are unknowable. An adverse NCLT outcome could affect the Bellary Facility I lease and A-One's 78.14% holding in Basai (S3).

No investor call, interview or numeric guidance from management was found in the sources reviewed. The forward-looking content in the RHP summaries is qualitative. Management points to continued Koppal logistics and processing upgrades (S28), a 10 MW power plant under construction and a waste-heat recovery system on 39.29 acres (S27), and further green-power sourcing under 15-25 year PPAs (S27). The Koppal expansion itself is described as debt-funded, without a disclosed capacity, cost or timeline in the reviewed coverage (S14).

items: Debt: Rs 250 cr prepayment planned in FY27 (S20).
Corporate simplification: amalgamation of Basai Steels and A-One Gold Pipes & Tubes into the company, pending NCLT approval (S7).
Industry backdrop: CRISIL projects 6.5-8.5% annual finished-steel demand growth from FY27 to FY31 (S8).

blocks.text: There is no concrete management outlook to lean on. Any growth view would have to be inferred from the FY26 margin spike and industry demand, and that is not a sound basis for an investment.

subsections.title: What would have to go right

blocks.text: For the bull case to work, three things must happen. FY26's roughly 7.3% EBITDA margin must hold through the steel cycle; it was 4.5-4.9% in FY24-FY25 (computed from S4, S6). Cash conversion must return, from FY26 OCF of Rs 62.80 cr towards the profit line (S6). And the Basai disputes must be resolved without loss of the Bellary Facility I site (S7). The first depends on the cycle, and the third depends on courts. Only the second is within management's control, and it will be visible in the first few listed quarters.
Sell-side and aggregator reviews stress 'green steel' and integration (S10, S15). Those are real features, but they do not change the unit economics of a commodity producer.

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: On September 23, 2026 the company allotted 29,85,160 shares at Rs 405 to 11 anchor investors, raising Rs 120.90 cr (S23, S12). The largest allocations went to LRSD Securities (Rs 28.40 cr, 23.49%), Morgan Stanley Asia (Rs 25.00 cr, 20.68%) and Longthrive Capital (Rs 20.00 cr, 16.54%) (S23). Taurus Mutual Fund was the only domestic mutual fund, at 4.14% across four schemes (S12). Half of the anchor shares (14,92,580) are locked in for 30 days and half for 90 days (S23).

The report is written on September 24, the first day of bidding. Category-wise subscription figures were not yet published on the tracker checked (S23). One aggregator's claim of '5.69x on the final day' could not be verified and is ignored, because the issue has not closed. Day-1 figures, when they appear, are partial and should not be read as a signal.

blocks.caption: Unofficial grey market premium readings (not an investment signal)

blocks.text: The anchor book is dominated by lightly known foreign and trading-style names, with only one domestic mutual fund (S23, S12). GMP is unofficial, varies widely across sources and is excluded from the verdict.

Red Herring Prospectus (company-hosted)

method: Research was done on 2026-09-24, the day the issue opened. The primary documents were identified: the SEBI DRHP filing page (S1), the SEBI addendum page (S2), the BSE-hosted DRHP, and the company-hosted RHP (S30). The full RHP could not be read: it exceeds the fetch tool's 10 MB limit, and the BSE DRHP returned HTTP 403. The only primary offer document read in full was the August 7, 2025 Addendum to the DRHP (S3), which covers subsidiaries and Basai Steels litigation. Everything else in the RHP is taken from secondary summaries, and each material figure was cross-checked across at least two of them. Restated financials were checked across Chittorgarh, Bajaj Broking, ScanX, IPO Watch and Business Remedies. Objects were checked across FPJ, Whalesbook, HDFC Sky and Multibagg. Revenue mix and the RHP's risk disclosures come from Multibagg's RHP-based articles and Samco. Governance findings come from the DRHP addendum and Moneylife. Known discrepancies: (a) pre-issue promoter holding is 85.86% per Chittorgarh vs 85.56% per Multibagg and Groww; (b) ipoji and a2zipo list DRHP-era capex objects, while all RHP-based sources show only debt repayment and GCP, and the latter was used; (c) debt-to-equity is reported as 1.17x by several sources and as 2.70x by ScanX, which reflects different definitions; (d) the Rs 6,285.84 cr promoter personal-guarantee figure is reported as crore by Multibagg but could not be reconciled with about Rs 1,011 cr of borrowings. The exact GCP amount (about Rs 50 cr) comes from a single source, and offer expenses were not confirmed. Capacity-utilisation and supplier-concentration figures (S29) were seen only in web-search result excerpts, because the page returned 403. No management interview or investor call was found. Day-1 subscription data had not been published at the time of writing. Per instructions, all valuation figures (P/E, P/B, market cap multiples, peer multiples) were deliberately excluded.
